title: Machinery I built and then did not need
subtitle: Fixed-size epochs and dense slots were built so decode steps could be captured as CUDA graphs; profiling showed the vendor's executor already does it. What I kept, what I stopped relying on, and the rule I took from it

stats.label: host key-value offload, set aside as a rejected idea
class-aware batching on average, also rejected

lede: CUDA graphs capture a sequence of kernel launches once and replay it without launch overhead, and a decode loop that runs the same step hundreds of thousands of times looks like the ideal candidate. Capture has a condition, though: the shapes must be stable. So I built the machinery that would make the runtime's decode steps capturable. An epoch is a span of steps with a fixed number of active slots. Slots are dense, so a batch of a given size always has the same layout; the map from sequence to slot is a bit vector with constant-time lookup; and a change in key-value-cache bucket falls back to eager execution for that step without ending the epoch.
quote: Read the library before reimplementing it, and measure before building the thing the measurement would justify.
evidence: GPU profiling and performance analysis: CUDA graph replay measured against eager execution before capture was wired in, kernel time 30.77 against 30.81 billion nanoseconds.
TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM engineering: established that the vendor's executor already captures and replays graphs internally, so the planned graph-capture work was dropped.
Inference runtime design: epochs with a fixed slot count, dense slots and a constant-time bit-vector slot map, kept for slot integrity after their first purpose went away.
Performance benchmarking methodology: rejected ideas kept with their measurements, host key-value offload at -6.8% and class-aware batching at -7.5% on average and -36% at peak.
author: Corey James
